summary.undergrad: The [[brainstem]] connects the brain to the spinal cord and keeps you alive: it controls breathing, heart rate and consciousness. Use the [[sagittal]] view to see all three parts at once.
summary.med: Identify the midbrain, pons and medulla on the midline sagittal image, and the pituitary in the sella turcica.

text.undergrad: The top part of the brainstem. It helps control eye movements and relays signals for hearing and vision.
text.med: Contains the nuclei of [[cranial-nerve|cranial nerves]] III and IV, the red nuclei and substantia nigra; the cerebral aqueduct runs through it.

text.undergrad: The bulging middle part of the brainstem. "Pons" means bridge: it links the cerebrum with the cerebellum.
text.med: Contains nuclei of cranial nerves V to VIII and the pontine nuclei relaying to the cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncles.

text.undergrad: The lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. It controls breathing and heart rate.
text.med: Contains nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII and cardiorespiratory centres; the corticospinal tracts decussate at its lower end (pyramidal decussation).
Sits in the sella turcica below the optic chiasm, between the cavernous sinuses. A mass here can compress the chiasm and cause a bitemporal hemianopia.

A mass growing up from the structure at the marker would classically cause which visual field defect?

options: Monocular blindness on the same side

explanation.med: An upward-growing pituitary mass compresses the crossing nasal fibres in the optic chiasm, causing a bitemporal hemianopia.
